warmup.q: The shop's program handles each booking on its own virtual thread and calls Pedal Post's booking service, which takes 20 calls at once. A Saturday rush brings 5,000 bookings at once. What protects Pedal Post?
options: Nothing is needed: virtual threads are cheap, so 5,000 calls are fine
The JVM limits virtual threads to the number of processor cores
A semaphore bulkhead of 20 around the booking call
warmup.why: Virtual threads remove the cost of threads, not the limits of what they call. The JVM runs them on a few carrier threads, but a virtual thread that waits steps off its carrier, so all 5,000 can be waiting on Pedal Post at once. A bulkhead, a semaphore with tryAcquire, caps the calls on the line at what the courier allows.

opening:
Saturday morning is the corner shop's busiest hour. Orders arrive faster than anyone can pack them, so the counter clips each slip onto a rail, and four packers take them off. At closing time, each packer must be sent home. At ten o'clock, the Big Blue Vans booking line goes quiet, and every call hangs for two seconds, then fails. Pedal Post's line takes twenty calls at once.

Every pattern so far was about one object. On a busy morning, many threads (paths of work that run side by side) use those objects at once. The concurrency track met this scene in a kitchen: the rail of tickets, the team of cooks, the price board nobody writes on, the ticket that says what to do next. The trap is to think cheap threads make everything cheap. The van company's line doesn't get any wider.

The last lesson ended on a busy Saturday. In this lesson, we'll name the concurrency patterns behind it, then build two from this track's patterns: a bulkhead, which caps the calls to one service, and a circuit breaker, which stops calling one that keeps failing. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started on a busy Saturday: a rail of slips, four packers, twenty phone lines and a van company that went quiet. The rail became a bounded queue with a card for each packer, the phone lines a semaphore, and the fuse box a breaker built from State, Decorator and an atomic reference.

That ends the track. Look in your own code for a call to another service with no limit around it and no timeout. That call is a van company waiting to go quiet.

Next, we'll look closely at the records we've used all through this track. A record looks like a short way to write a class. What exactly does it promise?

sections.h: The packing rail: producer-consumer and a team of packers
sections.html:
The safest way to share work between threads is to share a queue and nothing else. A queue is a line of items that leave in the order they joined. In producer-consumer, producers put work into a queue, consumers take it out, and the queue does all the locking (letting one thread in at a time) and waiting. At the shop, the counter is the producer, the packers are the consumers, and the rail of order slips is the queue: the kitchen rail from wait, notify and guarded blocks, moved to the back room. Java's BlockingQueue is that kind of queue for threads, and team below is a pool of threads that runs each packer. Kotlin's Channel is the same queue for coroutines, light tasks that can pause without holding a thread:

Java
BlockingQueue<Card> rail = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16);       // bounded: a full rail makes the counter wait
for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) {
    team.submit(() -> {
        while (true) {
            if (rail.take() instanceof Closed) return null;      // the poison pill: this packer goes home
            packed.incrementAndGet();
        }
    });
}
for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) rail.put(new Slip(i));
for (int p = 0; p < 4; p++) rail.put(new Closed());             // one card PER packer
Kotlin
val rail = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16)                         // bounded: send waits when the rail is full
val packers = List(4) {
    launch(Dispatchers.Default) {
        for (slip in rail) packed.incrementAndGet()            // ends when the rail is closed and empty
    }
}
repeat(1_000) { rail.send(it) }
rail.close()                                                   // one call sends every packer home

ProducerConsumerDemo, in the Try it, clips 1,000 slips onto a rail that holds 16, with four packers taking them off:

packed 1000 of 1000, all packers finished: true

Three rules from Classic problems: producer-consumer, philosophers, readers-writers still hold. Bound the queue: a full ArrayBlockingQueue(16) makes a fast counter wait, which is called backpressure, while an unbounded queue hides a pile-up until memory runs out. Send one poison pill, a special item that tells one consumer to stop, for each consumer, because each take() removes exactly one. And don't swallow InterruptedException: it's how a pool tells its threads to stop. Kotlin's channel needs no pill: close() ends every for (slip in rail) loop once the rail is empty. Use a for loop in each packer, not consumeEach, which cancels the whole channel when its own loop ends.

The rail picture holds until closing time. A packer can see the lights go off; a thread waiting in take() sees nothing until an item arrives, so you must send it one. Forget a card, and three packers wait by the empty rail all night.

A worker pool, or thread pool, is the same picture with the rail inside an ExecutorService: the team of cooks from Why pools: Executor, ExecutorService and shutdown, hired once. A fixed pool of ordinary threads still suits work that keeps the processor busy. For work that mostly waits, Java 21 brought back thread-per-message: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() starts a virtual thread, a cheap thread the JVM manages itself, for every task, and in Kotlin you launch a coroutine per message. Both make it easy to send ten thousand bookings at once to a courier who takes twenty.

Share a bounded queue and nothing else. Close it, or send one pill per consumer.

So thread-per-message always comes with a limit, and that limit is the bulkhead, two sections down. First, the patterns that keep state apart.

try.title: Forget a closed card
steps: Run ProducerConsumerDemo (Java or Kotlin) with the command below.
Java: replace the card loop with a single rail.put(new Closed());. Kotlin: delete rail.close(). Predict both parts of the output line, then run.

code.title: ProducerConsumerDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.BlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** The packing rail: the counter clips order slips on, four packers take them off, and each packer needs its own "closed" card. */ public class ProducerConsumerDemo { sealed interface Card permits Slip, Closed {} record Slip(int orderNo) implements Card {} record Closed() implements Card {} // the poison pill: "the shop is closed, go home" public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { int packers = 4, orders = 1_000; BlockingQueue<Card> rail = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(16); // bounded: a full rail makes the counter wait AtomicInteger packed = new AtomicInteger(); ExecutorService team = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(); for (int p = 0; p < packers; p++) { team.submit(() -> { while (true) { Card c = rail.take(); if (c instanceof Closed) return null; // this packer goes home packed.incrementAndGet(); } }); } for (int i = 0; i < orders; i++) rail.put(new Slip(i)); for (int p = 0; p < packers; p++) rail.put(new Closed()); // one card PER packer team.shutdown(); boolean finished = team.awaitTermination(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("packed " + packed + " of " + orders + ", all packers finished: " + finished); if (!finished) { team.shutdownNow(); // interrupt the ones still waiting in take() System.out.println("some packers never got a card and were still waiting at the rail"); } } }

alt.title: ProducerConsumerDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.Dispatchers import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel import kotlinx.coroutines.joinAll import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.withTimeoutOrNull import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds // The packing rail: the counter sends order slips, four packers take them, and close() sends every packer home. fun main() = runBlocking { val orders = 1_000 val rail = Channel<Int>(capacity = 16) // bounded: send suspends when the rail is full val packed = AtomicInteger() val packers = List(4) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { for (slip in rail) packed.incrementAndGet() // ends when the rail is closed and empty } } repeat(orders) { rail.send(it) } rail.close() // one call sends every packer home val finished = withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { packers.joinAll() } != null println("packed $packed of $orders, all packers finished: $finished") if (!finished) { packers.forEach { it.cancel() } println("the packers were still waiting at the rail: nobody closed it") } }

try.expect: packed 1000 of 1000, all packers finished: true. With one card, all 1,000 slips are still packed, but after the two-second wait the line reads all packers finished: false, and the demo reports that packers were still waiting at the rail: three of the four never got a card. In Kotlin without close(), the packers wait for a slip that never comes, and you get all packers finished: false too. In a real program, that is a shutdown that hangs.

sections.h: Who owns the state: the patterns you already know, and balking
sections.html:
Most of the other concurrency patterns answer one question: who owns this state, and what happens to a thread that arrives at the wrong moment? You've met them all in earlier tracks. Each row names a pattern, what it solves, and where you saw it:

Pattern What it solves Java 21+ Kotlin Taught in
Immutable object share state with no locks, like the price board nobody writes on records with List.copyOf data class with vals and copied lists Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal
Active object one owner for changeable state, like the stock worker that alone touches the shelves a single-thread executor as a mailbox; methods return CompletableFuture a coroutine that owns the state and reads commands from a Channel Observer and Command
Guarded suspension wait until a condition holds, like a cook waiting for the next ticket wait() in a while loop, or better CompletableFuture, CountDownLatch, Condition CompletableDeferred.await(), which suspends wait, notify and guarded blocks
Balking don't start a job that's already running AtomicBoolean.compareAndSet(false, true) the same, or Mutex.tryLock() Atomics and compare-and-set
Read-write lock many readers, rare writers ReentrantReadWriteLock (no read-to-write upgrade), or an AtomicReference to an immutable snapshot the same Explicit locks: ReentrantLock, Condition, ReadWriteLock
Future a result that arrives later, like the ticket that says what to do when the steak is ready CompletableFuture with your own executor async and await inside coroutineScope CompletableFuture: composing async steps

Balking means returning at once, instead of waiting, when the object isn't ready for the job, and it's the one people get wrong most often. The shop's stock count walks every shelf and counts what's left. It runs at closing time, again after a failure, and whenever the manager presses a button, and it must never run twice at once. If a count is already running, the right answer is to return at once:

Java
final class StockCount {
    private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean();

    boolean runIfIdle(Runnable count) {
        if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false;      // balk: a count is already running
        try {
            count.run();
            return true;
        } finally {
            running.set(false);
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class StockCount {
    private val mutex = Mutex()                                     // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex

    suspend fun runIfIdle(count: suspend () -> Unit): Boolean {
        if (!mutex.tryLock()) return false                          // balk: a count is already running
        try {
            count()
            return true
        } finally {
            mutex.unlock()
        }
    }
}

The Kotlin version uses a Mutex, a lock for coroutines, whose tryLock() gives up at once instead of waiting; the Kotlin twin of the demo keeps the AtomicBoolean, exactly as Java does. StockCountDemo, in the Try it, fires eight triggers at the same moment:

ran 1, balked 7, most counts at once: 1

The plain-boolean version, if (running) return; running = true;, is check-then-act, the race from Race conditions: why count++ lies: two threads can both see false before either one sets true, and two counts walk the same shelves at once. And an AtomicBoolean protects one program only. If the shop runs its program on two computers, each has its own flag, so a count that must be unique everywhere needs a shared lock, such as a row locked in the shop's database.

Balk with one atomic step, compareAndSet, never with a check and then a set.

Balking protects a job from itself. Next, we'll protect the services the shop calls from the shop.

try.title: Turn the balk into check-then-act
steps: Run StockCountDemo in either language: eight triggers fire at the same moment. Read the line.

Replace the compareAndSet line with three lines: if (running.get()) return false;, then for (int i = 0; i < 1_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); (Kotlin: repeat(1_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() }), then running.set(true);.
Run it four or five times and watch most counts at once. Then put the compareAndSet back.

code.title: StockCountDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the stock count refuses to start while one is already running. */ public class StockCountDemo { static final class StockCount { private final AtomicBoolean running = new AtomicBoolean(); boolean runIfIdle(Runnable count) { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false; // balk: a count is already running try { count.run(); return true; } finally { running.set(false); } } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { StockCount stockCount = new StockCount(); AtomicInteger inside = new AtomicInteger(), mostAtOnce = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger ran = new AtomicInteger(), balked = new AtomicInteger(); Runnable count = () -> { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); for (int i = 0; i < 2_000_000; i++) Thread.onSpinWait(); // counting the shelves takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet(); }; CountDownLatch go = new CountDownLatch(1); Thread[] triggers = new Thread[8]; // the closing-time timer, the manager's button, a retry... for (int t = 0; t < triggers.length; t++) { triggers[t] = new Thread(() -> { try { go.await(); } catch (InterruptedException e) { return; } if (stockCount.runIfIdle(count)) ran.incrementAndGet(); else balked.incrementAndGet(); }); triggers[t].start(); } go.countDown(); for (Thread t : triggers) t.join(); System.out.println("ran " + ran + ", balked " + balked + ", most counts at once: " + mostAtOnce); } }

alt.title: StockCountDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicBoolean import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Balking: eight triggers fire at once, and the stock count refuses to start while one is already running. class StockCount { private val running = AtomicBoolean() fun runIfIdle(count: () -> Unit): Boolean { if (!running.compareAndSet(false, true)) return false // balk: a count is already running try { count() return true } finally { running.set(false) } } } fun main() { val stockCount = StockCount() val inside = AtomicInteger() val mostAtOnce = AtomicInteger() val ran = AtomicInteger() val balked = AtomicInteger() val count = { mostAtOnce.accumulateAndGet(inside.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) repeat(2_000_000) { Thread.onSpinWait() } // counting the shelves takes a moment inside.decrementAndGet() Unit } val go = CountDownLatch(1) val triggers = List(8) { // the closing-time timer, the manager's button, a retry... thread { go.await() if (stockCount.runIfIdle(count)) ran.incrementAndGet() else balked.incrementAndGet() } } go.countDown() triggers.forEach { it.join() } println("ran $ran, balked $balked, most counts at once: $mostAtOnce") }

try.expect: With compareAndSet, most counts at once is always 1, and usually ran 1, balked 7. With check-then-act, several triggers pass the check before any of them sets the flag, so most runs print 2 or 3 for most counts at once: two stock counts walking the same shelves at the same time. It is the race from the concurrency track, inside a pattern.

sections.h: Bulkhead: a fixed number of phone lines for each service
sections.html:
Virtual threads make threads cheap. They don't make the services the shop calls any bigger. A service here is another program the shop's program calls over the network, such as a courier's booking line or the shop's database. Pedal Post's booking line takes 20 calls at once, the database accepts 20 connections, and Big Blue Vans slows to a crawl above 50. A bulkhead caps how many calls run against one service at once, so a slow service can use up its own share and nothing else. The name comes from ships, where watertight walls keep one leak from flooding the whole hull.

The shop's picture is a switchboard. Pedal Post has 20 phone lines. When all 20 are busy, a caller hears the busy tone at once and can try something else, instead of waiting on hold with the music. In code, the lines are the permits of a semaphore, a counter of permits that threads take and give back:

Java
final class Bulkhead {
    private final Semaphore permits;
    Bulkhead(int maxConcurrent) { permits = new Semaphore(maxConcurrent); }

    <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull("all lines busy");   // busy tone: fail fast
        try {
            return op.get();
        } finally {
            permits.release();                                  // always, or the shop loses a line for good
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class Bulkhead(maxConcurrent: Int) {
    private val permits = Semaphore(maxConcurrent)              // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore

    suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T {
        if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull("all lines busy")        // busy tone: fail fast
        try {
            return op()
        } finally {
            permits.release()                                   // always, or the shop loses a line for good
        }
    }
}

BulkheadDemo, in the Try it, sends 200 bookings that each take 20 ms through 20 lines, first waiting on hold (acquire()), then with the busy tone (tryAcquire()). One run, on a busy machine, printed:

wait       done 200, rejected   0, most at once 20, about 288 ms
fail fast  done  20, rejected 180, most at once 20, about 26 ms

Correctness first: neither mode ever had more than 20 calls on the line. Then time. Waiting served all 200 in about ten rounds of 20, close to 300 ms. Failing fast answered every caller within about 26 ms, and 180 of them heard the busy tone. Your numbers will differ a little; the shape won't.

tryAcquire() makes the bulkhead fail fast: a call over the limit gets an error at once instead of waiting behind the slow ones. acquire() waits, which turns the bulkhead into a limiter. That's fine for a job that runs at night, and risky for a customer at the counter, where waiting calls pile up until someone gives up.

Size each bulkhead to its service, not to your threads. A bulkhead of 30 in front of a database with 20 connections still makes ten callers wait inside. With virtual threads, a semaphore is the natural limit, as in Using virtual threads: one per task, limits with semaphores, where the grill had room for 20 pans.

The switchboard picture breaks when the call ends. A phone line frees itself when the caller hangs up. A permit comes back only if your code gives it back, which is why release() sits in finally: miss it once on an exception, and the shop has 19 lines for good.

Give each service its own bulkhead, sized to what that service can take, and release in finally.

A bulkhead limits how much a slow service can hurt the shop. A service that's down needs something stronger.

try.title: Wait on hold, or hear the busy tone
steps: Run BulkheadDemo (Java or Kotlin). It sends 200 bookings that each take 20 ms through a 20-permit semaphore, first with acquire() (wait), then with tryAcquire() (fail fast). Predict both lines first.
Change the semaphore from 20 permits to 200 and run again. Predict most at once before you look.

code.title: BulkheadDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l11; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Semaphore; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger; /** 200 virtual threads book a courier whose booking line takes at most 20 calls at once: wait for a free line, or fail fast. */ public class BulkheadDemo { static void run(String mode, boolean failFast) throws InterruptedException { Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(20); AtomicInteger onLine = new AtomicInteger(), mostOnLine = new AtomicInteger(); AtomicInteger done = new AtomicInteger(), rejected = new AtomicInteger(); long start = System.nanoTime(); try (ExecutorService ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { for (int i = 0; i < 200; i++) { ex.submit(() -> { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return null; } // bulkhead: busy tone, at once } else { permits.acquire(); // limiter: wait on hold } try { mostOnLine.accumulateAndGet(onLine.incrementAndGet(), Math::max); Thread.sleep(20); // a booking takes 20 ms onLine.decrementAndGet(); done.incrementAndGet(); } finally { permits.release(); } return null; }); } } // close() waits for all tasks long ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000; System.out.printf("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most at once %2d, about %d ms%n", mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostOnLine.get(), ms); } public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { run("wait", false); run("fail fast", true); } }

alt.title: BulkheadDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l11 import kotlinx.coroutines.coroutineScope import kotlinx.coroutines.delay import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger // 200 coroutines book a courier whose booking line takes at most 20 calls at once: wait for a free line, or fail fast. suspend fun runBulkhead(mode: String, failFast: Boolean) { val permits = Semaphore(20) val onLine = AtomicInteger() val mostOnLine = AtomicInteger() val done = AtomicInteger() val rejected = AtomicInteger() val start = System.nanoTime() coroutineScope { // waits for all 200 children repeat(200) { launch { if (failFast) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) { rejected.incrementAndGet(); return@launch } // bulkhead: busy tone, at once } else { permits.acquire() // limiter: wait on hold } try { mostOnLine.accumulateAndGet(onLine.incrementAndGet(), ::maxOf) delay(20) // a booking takes 20 ms onLine.decrementAndGet() done.incrementAndGet() } finally { permits.release() } } } } val ms = (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000_000 println("%-10s done %3d, rejected %3d, most at once %2d, about %d ms".format(mode, done.get(), rejected.get(), mostOnLine.get(), ms)) } fun main() = runBlocking { runBulkhead("wait", failFast = false) runBulkhead("fail fast", failFast = true) }

try.expect: Waiting: done 200, rejected 0, most at once 20, in a bit over 200 ms (ten rounds of 20). Fail fast: about done 20, rejected 180, in 20 to 30 ms. The exact split can vary slightly between runs. With 200 permits, most at once jumps to 200 in both modes: nothing protects the courier. Your times will differ a little from these.

sections.h: Circuit breaker: State, Decorator and compare-and-set in one class
sections.html:
At ten o'clock, the Big Blue Vans booking service goes quiet. Every call hangs for two seconds and then fails, and the customers at the counter wait each time. The shop's back room has a fuse box with a circuit breaker: when something goes wrong in the wiring, it trips and cuts the power, so the fault can't do more damage. The software circuit breaker borrows the name. After a run of failures it opens, and calls fail at once without even trying the van company. After a cool-down, it goes half-open and lets one test call through, called a probe. Success closes it again; failure opens it for another cool-down.

The breaker is this track's capstone, because it is three earlier patterns in one class. Its states are sealed records with a transition, as in State and Chain of Responsibility. Its call(op) wraps any operation and keeps its shape, as a decorator does in Decorator and Proxy. And its state lives in an AtomicReference, a holder for one object that threads can swap safely, and changes by compare-and-set, read as "update it only if nobody beat me to it", so a thousand threads can share it without a lock:

Java
sealed interface State permits Closed, Open, HalfOpen {}
record Closed(int consecutiveFailures) implements State {}
record Open(Instant until) implements State {}
record HalfOpen() implements State {}

private final AtomicReference<State> state = new AtomicReference<>(new Closed(0));

// after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically
state.updateAndGet(cur -> switch (cur) {
    case HalfOpen h -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor));                            // the probe failed
    case Closed(var n) when n + 1 >= threshold -> new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)); // trip
    case Closed(var n) -> new Closed(n + 1);
    case Open o -> o;                                                                      // already open
});
Kotlin
sealed interface State {
    data class Closed(val consecutiveFailures: Int) : State
    data class Open(val until: Instant) : State
    data object HalfOpen : State
}

private val state = AtomicReference<State>(State.Closed(0))

// after a failed call: one pure transition, applied atomically
state.updateAndGet { cur ->
    when (cur) {
        State.HalfOpen -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor)                                     // the probe failed
        is State.Closed if cur.consecutiveFailures + 1 >= threshold -> State.Open(clock.instant() + openFor)   // trip
        is State.Closed -> State.Closed(cur.consecutiveFailures + 1)
        is State.Open -> cur                                                                        // already open
    }
}

Two choices make it testable and correct. Time comes from a Clock passed in through the constructor, so a test can hand it a fake clock and move time forward 31 seconds at once instead of sleeping. And the move from open to half-open is a compareAndSet: when the cool-down ends and many threads arrive together, exactly one wins the right to probe, and the rest are still turned away. The figure shows the three states and the moves between them.

The fuse box picture breaks in two places. A real breaker stays off until a person resets it; the software one tries again by itself after the cool-down. And a real breaker reacts to the current in the wire, while the software one only counts failures, so you must tell it which errors mean "the service is sick". A courier who answers "no vans free in your area" is working perfectly, and must not trip the breaker.

Count only the failures that mean the service is sick, and let one probe, chosen by compare-and-set, decide when it has recovered.

Check yourself. The breaker opened at 10:00:00 with a 30-second cool-down. A test moves the fake clock to 10:00:31, and eight threads call at the same moment. How many calls reach the van company, and what picks them? (One. Each thread tries the compareAndSet from Open to HalfOpen; exactly one succeeds and runs the probe. The other seven find the state already changed and are turned away.)

aside.title: Should I build my own breaker?
aside.html: Only to learn how one works, as the lab does. In a real program, use a library. Resilience4j, a fault-tolerance library for Java (2.4.0 when this course was written), gives you breakers with sliding windows, failure-rate and slow-call thresholds, metrics and events, plus bulkheads and retries. Learn its defaults before you trust a test: minimumNumberOfCalls is 100, so a breaker that fails five calls in a unit test never opens, and waitDurationInOpenState is 60 seconds. Its semaphore bulkhead fails fast by default, like ours: maxConcurrentCalls is 25 and maxWaitDuration is 0.

video.title: A circuit breaker's three states live in one AtomicReference, and compare-and-set picks the single probe

compare.title: Guarded suspension: waiting for the courier to confirm a pickup

java.title: PickupConfirmations.java
java.html: // the counter's thread waits until the courier confirms the pickup, or gives up after a timeout final class PickupConfirmations { private final ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableFuture<String>> pending = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(); String awaitConfirmation(String orderNo, Duration timeout) throws InterruptedException, ExecutionException, TimeoutException { CompletableFuture<String> slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo, no -> new CompletableFuture<>()); try { return slot.get(timeout.toMillis(), TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS); // blocks this thread until completed } finally { pending.remove(orderNo); } } // the courier's message arrives on another thread; one that comes first is kept for the waiter void onConfirmation(String orderNo, String pickupRef) { pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo, no -> new CompletableFuture<>()).complete(pickupRef); } }

kotlin.title: PickupConfirmations.kt
kotlin.html: // the counter's coroutine waits until the courier confirms the pickup, or gives up after a timeout class PickupConfirmations { private val pending = ConcurrentHashMap<String, CompletableDeferred<String>>() suspend fun awaitConfirmation(orderNo: String, timeout: Duration): String { val slot = pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo) { CompletableDeferred() } try { return withTimeout(timeout) { slot.await() } // suspends: no thread is held while waiting } finally { pending.remove(orderNo) } } // the courier's message arrives elsewhere; one that comes first is kept for the waiter fun onConfirmation(orderNo: String, pickupRef: String) { pending.computeIfAbsent(orderNo) { CompletableDeferred() }.complete(pickupRef) } }

compare.note: Both replace the hand-written wait() in a while loop with a one-shot promise, which can't miss a signal or wake up by accident: complete happens once, and get or await returns as soon as it has. The difference is what waiting costs. CompletableFuture.get blocks a thread; on a virtual thread that is cheap, but it is still a thread per waiting order. CompletableDeferred.await suspends the coroutine and holds no thread at all, and withTimeout cancels the wait cleanly. Java needs three checked exceptions in the signature; Kotlin needs none, and the timeout arrives as a TimeoutCancellationException. One gap is shared: a confirmation that arrives after the waiter gave up leaves an entry in the map, so a real version also clears out old entries.

worked.title: Put retry, breaker and bulkhead in the right order

steps.say: Three pieces from this lesson wrap one van booking. The order of the wrappers decides what happens on a bad morning. Before reading on: with the retry on the outside, what does each attempt do while the breaker is open?
steps.code: Supplier<String> book = () -> vans.book("order-7781", 2); // safe to repeat: the van company skips a second booking for 7781 Supplier<String> limited = () -> bulkhead.call(book); // innermost: caps the calls on the line Supplier<String> guarded = () -> breaker.call(limited); // then: stop calling a service that keeps failing String ref = retrying(3, guarded); // outermost: try again after a passing failure

alt.html: val book = Supplier { vans.book("order-7781", 2) } // safe to repeat: the van company skips a second booking for 7781 val limited = Supplier { bulkhead.call(book) } // innermost: caps the calls on the line val guarded = Supplier { breaker.call(limited) } // then: stop calling a service that keeps failing val ref = retrying(3) { guarded.get() } // outermost: try again after a passing failure

steps.say: Each attempt hits the open breaker and gets CallNotPermitted in microseconds, which costs the van company nothing. But a rejection isn't a passing failure, and retrying it is noise. Teach the retry to let the fail-fast signals through untouched.
steps.code: static <T> T retrying(int attempts, Supplier<T> body) { RuntimeException last = null; for (int i = 1; i <= attempts; i++) { try { return body.get(); } catch (CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted | Bulkhead.BulkheadFull e) { throw e; // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (RuntimeException e) { last = e; // 2. a timeout or a dropped line: worth another try } } throw last; }

alt.html: inline fun <T> retrying(attempts: Int, body: () -> T): T { var last: RuntimeException? = null repeat(attempts) { try { return body() } catch (e: CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted) { throw e // 1. fail-fast signals: never retry them } catch (e: Bulkhead.BulkheadFull) { throw e } catch (e: RuntimeException) { last = e // 2. a timeout or a dropped line: worth another try } } throw last!! }

steps.say: Why is the bulkhead inside the breaker? An open breaker turns calls away before they reach the bulkhead, so a dead service never holds a line. Why is the retry outside? Each attempt is a separate breaker call, so three failed attempts count as three failures, and a van company that is really down trips the breaker within one or two bookings. A retry inside the breaker would hide those failures from it.
steps.code:
what each layer sees for one booking while the van company is down:

retry      attempt 1          attempt 2          attempt 3
breaker    Closed(0) -> (1)   Closed(1) -> (2)   Closed(2) -> Open    (three failures trip it)
bulkhead   line, given back   line, given back   line, given back

next booking: retry -> breaker turns it away at once (CallNotPermitted) -> no call, no line used

steps.say: Pin it in a test, with a fake van service that always fails and the lab's classes. The second booking must never reach the van company.
steps.code: AtomicInteger vanCalls = new AtomicInteger(); Supplier<String> failing = () -> { vanCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw new IllegalStateException("vans booking line down"); }; CircuitBreaker breaker = new CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock); Bulkhead bulkhead = new Bulkhead(20); Supplier<String> pipeline = () -> breaker.call(() -> bulkhead.call(failing)); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).hasMessage("vans booking line down"); // 3. first booking: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open.class); assertThatThrownBy(() -> retrying(3, pipeline)).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted.class); assertThat(vanCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3); // 4. the second never left

alt.html: val vanCalls = AtomicInteger() val failing = Supplier<String> { vanCalls.incrementAndGet(); throw IllegalStateException("vans booking line down") } val breaker = CircuitBreaker(3, Duration.ofSeconds(30), clock) val bulkhead = Bulkhead(20) val pipeline = { breaker.call { bulkhead.call(failing) } } assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.hasMessage("vans booking line down") // 3. first booking: 3 attempts assertThat(breaker.state()).isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.Open::class.java) assertThatThrownBy { retrying(3, pipeline) }.isInstanceOf(CircuitBreaker.CallNotPermitted::class.java) assertThat(vanCalls.get()).isEqualTo(3) // 4. the second never left

lab.title: A circuit breaker with a fake clock, and a semaphore bulkhead
steps: Read the state table in the Javadoc of CircuitBreaker; the states, the constructor and state() are given. Run the tests: all ten fail.

Write the first half of call: read the state. If it is Open and the clock is still before until, throw CallNotPermitted. If the cool-down is over, compareAndSet it to HalfOpen, and throw if you lose. If it is already HalfOpen, throw.

Write the second half: run op. On success, move to Closed(0) unless another thread has opened the breaker in the meantime. On a RuntimeException, apply the failure transition with updateAndGet and rethrow the same exception.
Run the tests until all ten pass, then run them twice more. Code that many threads share has to pass every time.
hints: if (s instanceof Open(var until)) gives you until in one step. state.compareAndSet(s, new HalfOpen()) succeeds only if nobody changed the state since you read s, so exactly one thread becomes the probe.
On success, state.updateAndGet(cur -> cur instanceof Open ? cur : new Closed(0)) closes both a half-open breaker and a closed one with failures, without undoing an open set by another thread.
The failure transition is the four-case switch from the lesson: HalfOpen and the tripping Closed both become new Open(clock.instant().plus(openFor)).
lab.done: All ten tests in ResilienceTest pass, three runs in a row.

drill.title: A fail-fast bulkhead from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a Bulkhead that lets at most n calls run at once and turns the rest away immediately with an exception. Then answer two questions: what goes wrong if you release() outside a finally, and what changes if you use acquire() instead of tryAcquire()?

answer.html: final class Bulkhead { static final class BulkheadFull extends RuntimeException {} private final Semaphore permits; Bulkhead(int n) { permits = new Semaphore(n); } <T> T call(Supplier<T> op) { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw new BulkheadFull(); // fail fast; acquire() would wait on hold try { return op.get(); } finally { permits.release(); // outside finally, every exception loses a permit until none are left } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class Bulkhead(n: Int) { class BulkheadFull : RuntimeException() private val permits = Semaphore(n) // kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore suspend fun <T> call(op: suspend () -> T): T { if (!permits.tryAcquire()) throw BulkheadFull() // fail fast; acquire() would suspend on hold try { return op() } finally { permits.release() // outside finally, every exception loses a permit until none are left } } }

recap: Producer-consumer: share a bounded queue and nothing else. One poison pill per consumer in Java; close() the channel in Kotlin, with a for loop, not consumeEach, in each worker.
Thread-per-message is back with virtual threads and coroutines, but cheap threads make it easy to flood a service, so it always comes with a limit.
Balking returns at once when a job is already running. Use compareAndSet (or Mutex.tryLock), never a check-then-act on a plain boolean.
A bulkhead is a semaphore per service with tryAcquire: it fails fast, releases in finally, and is sized to the service, not to your threads.

A circuit breaker is State plus Decorator plus compare-and-set: sealed states in an AtomicReference, a call(op) wrapper, an injected Clock, and one half-open probe chosen by compareAndSet. Retry in one layer only, outside the breaker, and never on a rejection.

The limit: each of these lives in one program's memory. Two copies of the program have two flags, two bulkheads and two breakers, so a limit for the whole shop needs something they share, such as a lock in the database.

explain.prompt: Explain how the lab's circuit breaker combines State, Decorator and compare-and-set, and why the move from open to half-open has to be a compareAndSet.
explain.answer: The breaker's state is a small sealed type, Closed(failures), Open(until) and HalfOpen, and each outcome moves it with a pure transition, like the order's life in State and Chain of Responsibility. That's State. Its call(op) takes any operation and returns that operation's result through the same shape, adding behavior around it, which is what a decorator does. The current state lives in an AtomicReference, so hundreds of threads can share one breaker without a lock, and every change is a compareAndSet or an updateAndGet. The open-to-half-open move matters most. When the cool-down ends, many threads may read the same expired Open state at once. compareAndSet(thatOpen, new HalfOpen()) succeeds for exactly one of them, which becomes the probe; the others see their compare-and-set fail and are turned away. With a plain set, every one of them would call a service that may still be down. The injected Clock is what lets the tests check all this without sleeping.

deeper.html:
Resilience4j's breaker defaults, read from its source and printed by version 2.4.0: failureRateThreshold 50%, slowCallRateThreshold 100%, slowCallDurationThreshold 60 s, waitDurationInOpenState 60 s, permittedNumberOfCallsInHalfOpenState 10, minimumNumberOfCalls 100, and a count-based sliding window of 100 calls. Every exception counts as a failure unless you configure recordExceptions or ignoreExceptions. The project's README says Resilience4j 3 will require Java 21 and adds virtual-thread schedulers; it wasn't on Maven Central when this course was written, so the labs build the breaker by hand.

Spring Framework 7, a widely used framework for Java web services, added @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit to its core, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. @Retryable defaults to maxRetries = 3 after the first failure, so four attempts in total, with a one-second delay. Both work through proxies, so the self-call rule from Decorator and Proxy applies: a method that calls another method on this skips them.

Structured concurrency is the future pattern with a lifetime. StructuredTaskScope starts subtasks, waits for them, and cancels the rest when one fails, so no subtask outlives the method that started it. It is still a preview API in JDK 25, 26 and 27 (run with --enable-preview), which is why it stays out of the labs. Kotlin's coroutineScope has worked this way from the start: an async that fails cancels its siblings, and the scope waits for every child.

The patterns in this lesson have cousins that span several programs. A lock held in a shared database is balking across copies of a program. A queue server, a separate program that holds messages until other programs take them, is producer-consumer between programs. The questions stay the same: who owns the state, what waits, and what fails fast.
